caption: Now the column holds true timestamps rather than strings — that unlocks everything else.

eyebrow: Ambiguous formats — state the format explicitly
code:
pd.to_datetime("03/04/2024")                   # 2024-03-04 (month first)
pd.to_datetime("03/04/2024", dayfirst=True)    # 2024-04-03
pd.to_datetime("04-03-24", format="%d-%m-%y")  # 2024-03-04
caption: Specifying format= is safest in production — it removes guessing about what 03/04/2024 means.

code:
s = pd.Series(["2024-01-05", "not a date"])
pd.to_datetime(s, errors="coerce")
# 0   2024-01-05
# 1          NaT
caption: NaT ("not a time") instead of a crash — then count the NaTs to see how much failed to parse.

code:
d = orders["order_date"]
d.dt.year          # 2024
d.dt.month         # 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3
d.dt.day_name()    # Friday, Sunday, Monday, ...
d.dt.dayofweek     # Monday = 0
caption: Build features like "is weekend" or "month of purchase" straight from these.
Compare a datetime column to a date string directly — pandas converts it for you. between() includes both ends.

code:
snapshot = pd.Timestamp("2024-03-31")
orders["days_ago"] = (snapshot - orders["order_date"]).dt.days

# order_date + pd.Timedelta(days=30)  -> a due date
caption: Subtracting two dates gives a Timedelta; .dt.days turns it into a number — the basis of recency measures.
